title: Greedy and lazy
summary: Why ".*" grabs from the first quote to the last, how the engine backtracks, lazy quantifiers, and the negated class that is faster and works in every tool.

steps.title: Greedy: take everything, then give back
body: Quantifiers are **greedy**: they take as much as they can, then give characters back one at a time until the rest
of the pattern matches. That giving back is called **backtracking**.
Watch `".*"` on `name="api" env="prod"`:
1. `"` matches the first quote.
2. `.*` runs to the end of the line: it eats `api" env="prod"`.
3. The final `"` has nothing left to match, so `.*` gives back one character, the last `"`. Now it matches.
The result is one match, `"api" env="prod"`, from the first quote to the **last**. Correct by the rules, and almost
never what you wanted. Press the debugger below and step through the giving back.

steps.explain: Every greedy quantifier runs as far as it can. `<.+>` does not stop at the first `>`: it runs to the end and gives back only as far as the last `>`.

steps.title: Lazy: take as little as possible
body: Add `?` after a quantifier to make it **lazy**: it takes as few characters as it can, and only takes one more when
the rest of the pattern fails.
| Greedy | Lazy | Lazy means |
| `*` | `*?` | zero or more, as few as possible |
| `+` | `+?` | one or more, as few as possible |
| `?` | `??` | prefer zero |
`".*?"` stops at the **first** closing quote, so it finds `"api"` and then `"prod"`. Step through it: after each
character the engine checks whether a `"` comes next.
Lazy and greedy only change **which** match is chosen. Neither can make a pattern match text it otherwise could not.

steps.title: Each quoted value, lazily
prompt: A config line holds several quoted values. Find each one, quotes included, as a separate match. Use a **lazy**
In `name="api" env="prod"` the matches must be exactly `"api"` and `"prod"`.
hints: Start from the greedy `".*"` and make the `*` lazy.
steps.explain: `.*?` grows one character at a time and stops as soon as a `"` can follow. With `+?` instead, the empty value `""` would be missed: `"" id="` would be one match.

steps.prompt: Each pattern runs on the text `aaa`. Match it to its first match.
steps.explain: A lazy quantifier takes its minimum first: one for `+?`, two for `{2,}?`, zero for `*?`. Nothing comes after it in the pattern, so the minimum already succeeds.

steps.title: Better still: say what may not appear
body: Seniors usually write the quoted-value pattern as `"[^"]*"`: a quote, any number of **non-quote** characters, a quote.
- **It says what you mean.** The value cannot contain a quote, so it cannot run past the closing one.
- **Less work for the engine.** `[^"]*` runs straight to the closing quote. A lazy `.*?` stops after every
character to test whether the rest matches. Step through both in the debugger and compare the step counts.
- **It works in every tool.** POSIX `grep -E`, `sed` and `awk` have no lazy quantifiers. `[^"]*` works in all of them,
in .NET, Python, JavaScript and rg.
One difference to know: `[^"]` also matches a newline, the dot does not. Usually you search line by line anyway.
The same trick for tags: `<[^>]+>`. For real HTML, JSON or CSV with escaped quotes, use a parser, not a regex.

steps.prompt: On a Linux server you run `grep -oE '<pattern>' app.conf` to print every quoted value. Which pattern gives one match per value?
steps.explain: POSIX extended regex has no lazy quantifiers. GNU grep reads `.*?` as "`.*`, optionally", which is still greedy, so it silently prints one long match per line. The negated class works everywhere. (`grep -P` and `rg` do support `.*?`.)

steps.title: Symptom: the audit report shows impossible user names
prompt: **Symptom.** The weekly audit report lists a user called `alice" role="admin" ip="10.0.0.7`. The extractor reads
audit lines like this one and captures the user name in the brackets of `user="(.*)"`:
(The parentheses capture the part between them as group 1. Module 4 covers groups.) Fix the pattern so group 1 is
just the user name, even when it is empty.
hints: The greedy `.*` runs to the end of the line and gives back only as far as the **last** quote.
Stop the value at the first quote: `user="([^"]*)"` (or a lazy `.*?`).
steps.explain: `[^"]*` cannot cross a quote, so the value ends where the user name does. A lazy `(.*?)` also passes. Note how the bug hid: on a line with only one quoted field, the greedy version worked, so it passed a quick test.

steps.title: Every quoted value
prompt: Write `List<string> QuotedValues(string line)` that returns every double-quoted value in `line`, **without** the
quotes, left to right. Use `Regex.Matches` with the negated class, then strip the first and last character of each
A quote inside a C# string needs escaping. Either form works:
var pattern = "\"[^\"]*\"";        // normal string: \" is a quote
var same    = @"""[^""]*""";       // verbatim string: "" is a quote
`QuotedValues("msg=\"disk full\" code=\"E42\"")` returns `["disk full", "E42"]`. An empty value `""` gives an
template: Dojo.Eq("two values", new List<string> { "api", "prod" }, QuotedValues("name=\"api\" env=\"prod\""));
Dojo.Eq("a value with a space", new List<string> { "disk full", "E42" }, QuotedValues("msg=\"disk full\" code=\"E42\""));
Dojo.Eq("an empty value", new List<string> { "", "7" }, QuotedValues("note=\"\" id=\"7\""));
Dojo.Eq("no quotes, no values", new List<string>(), QuotedValues("level=info"));
hints: `foreach (Match m in Regex.Matches(line, "\"[^\"]*\""))` visits each quoted value.
Add `m.Value[1..^1]` to the list: the range drops the first and last character.
